speakeroldname: Mr. R. N. Thompson (Red Deer) moved
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF ALASKA-YUKON HIGHWAY AUTHORITY
speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-112, to provide for the establishment of an Alaska-Yukon highway authority (Alaska highway).

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF ALASKA-YUKON HIGHWAY AUTHORITY
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF ALASKA-YUKON HIGHWAY AUTHORITY
speechtext:
This bill calls for the establishment of an Alaska-Yukon highway authority which would provide an alternative to the impasse which presently prevents any workable agreement being made between the government of the United States and the government of Canada, an impasse which apparently is holding up the completion and paving of this important national highway project.
This bill provides for the establishment of a special authority which would permit cooperation among the various governments at different levels so as to facilitate the completion of such a highway and enable the costs to be shared. This is particularly important to us at the present time because the Alaska centenary coincides with the centenary of Canada. Action along these lines would certainly provide what could be an important international aspect of the centenary year.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

[Mr. Matheson.l

Hon. Robert H. Winters (Minister of Trade
and Commerce): The only commercial agreement signed by Canada and the United States on December 17, 1965, concerned adjustments in the U.S. tariff and did not deal with imports into Canada of textiles or any other products.
The negotiations were made necessary by revisions in the U.S. tariff in 1963, principally designed to bring the U.S. tariff language up to date. There were, however, a number of incidental increases as well as decreases and these affected the balance of concessions which have been negotiated under the GATT. The agreement on December 17, 1965, involved a number of compensating reductions in the U.S. tariff and a re-binding to Canada of schedules of United States tariff in the GATT.
The announcement of this agreement and a list of the concessions in the U.S. tariff is attached.

subtopic: CANADA-U.S. TARIFF AGREEMENT

speechtext:
Ottawa, December 17,	1965-The Hon.
Mitchell Sharp, Minister of Trade and Commerce announced that an agreement was signed in Washington today respecting U.S. tariff concessions on Canadian goods under the revised United States tariff schedules which became effective August 31, 1963. The agreement provides for rebinding of previous U.S. concessions negotiated with Canada under the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade. The agreement also provides for reductions in U.S. tariffs on a range of products which accounted for approximately $32 million of Canadian exports to the United States in 1964.
For items covering over $20 million of Canadian exports in 1964, the agreement provides for reductions of up to 50 per cent in present rates of the U.S. tariff. These reductions are to be implemented over a four-year period commencing January 1, 1966. Canadian exports to the U.S. in 1964 of the main items benefitting from these cuts were: aircraft parts, $3.2 million (non-military); building boards, $2.7 million; vehicles such as house trailers and utility trailers, $2.5 million; metal structures e.g. buildings and transmission towers, $1.8 million; air conditioners and parts, $1.7 million; certain machinery parts e.g. pulleys, blocks, clutches, universal joints, chain sprockets, $1.5 million; tapes, cocks, valves, $0.9 million; radio, T.V.

These concessions have already been implemented as a result of U.S. legislation enacted in October this year. February 2, 1966

being placed on the construction industry in 1965 and 1966 as a means of sustaining a steady rate of economic growth throughout Canada. speechtext:
1. The act establishing the corporation under section 10 provides as follows:
(1)	The corporation shall, as soon as practicable and in any event not later than one year after the coming into force of this act, submit for the approval of the Governor in Council and the Lieutenant Governor in Council its over-all plan for the exhibition, setting forth the various undertakings and projects proposed by the corporation in connection with the planning, organizing, holding and administering of the exhibition, the estimated cost of each such undertaking or project and an estimate of the total capital costs and operating costs of the corporation in respect of the exhibition.
(2)	Any material changes in the plan referred to in subsection (1), including estimates of costs therein, shall be submitted by the corporation to the Governor in Council and the Lieutenant Governor in Council for approval.
(3)	Notwithstanding any other provision of this act and except for the purposes of subsections (1) and (2) the corporation shall not initiate any undertaking or project, expend any money thereon or incur any liability therefor unless that undertaking or project is included in the approved over-all plan for the exhibition or modification thereof.
The same act, under section 11, also provides as follows: "The Minister of Finance, at the request of the corporation, may, out of the consolidated revenue fund, pay to the corporation by way of grant such amounts as are required for the conduct of the business of the corporation but the aggregate of all amounts paid to the corporation under this section shall not exceed twenty million dollars."
The act contains further provisions under which the corporation may borrow funds to meet its corporate needs. Section 12 provides as follows:

speakeroldname: Hon. Leo Cadieux (Associate Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: PRINCESS LOUISE DRAGOON GUARDS
speechtext:
1. The Princess Louise Dragoon Guards originated as the "Ottawa Troop of Cavalry" authorized 23 May 1872 and redesignated "Dragoon Guards" on 15 November 1878 and as "The Princess Louise Dragoon Guards" on 3 January 1879. It became a regiment with the formation of an additional squadron and a regimental headquarters authorized respectively on 1 January 1903 and 1 February 1903. The regiment was redesignated "5 th Princess Louise Dragoon Guards" on 1 February 1903; "The Princess Louise Dragoon Guards" on 1 February 1903; "The Princess Louise Dragoon Guards" on 15 March 1920. It was amalgamated with the 4th Hussars of Canada on 15 December 1936 and redesignated "4th Princess Louise Dragoon Guards".
2.	The regiment has not been disbanded. It was reduced to nil strength and transferred to the supplementary order of battle effective 31 March 1965.
3.	The regiment was transferred to the supplementary order of battle following a review of the recommendations of the ministerial commission on the reorganization of the militia. The commission recommended that the Princess Louise Dragoon Guards be reduced to nil strength as there was no foreseeable requirement for the unit. The departmental review confirmed this recommendation.
4.	The Princess Louise Dragoon Guards is at present a unit of the Canadian Army (militia) supplementary order of battle. As such its name and traditions will be preserved in view of the valued contribution which the unit has made in the past and against the possibility that changed circumstances might require its reactivation in the future.

February 2, 1966

5.	Not at this time. The circumstances which gave rise to the regiment's transfer to the supplementary order of battle have not changed.

speechtext:

subtopic: SPEECH BY QUEBEC MINISTER RESPECTING U.S. RESTRICTIONS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: SPEECH BY QUEBEC MINISTER RESPECTING U.S. RESTRICTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I direct a question to the Minister of Finance. Has his attention been drawn to the very full and complete report of the speech given in Toronto by Hon. Eric Kierans? Indeed, the report is so full that most politicians would hope they might achieve the same results. Mr. Kierans has stated that the restrictions imposed by United States guide lines on Canadian economic policy are serious; that they are tightening the grip of the United States on our economy and they threaten the attainment of our own economic objectives.
In view of the high position held by Mr. Kierans and his widespread knowledge gained as a result of having been President of the Montreal Stock Exchange, are not his statements well founded? I do not want to get into an argument between the federal and provincial governments in any way. In view of the fact that the minister did not approve of the guide lines, what representations has the government of Canada made in this regard?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SPEECH BY QUEBEC MINISTER RESPECTING U.S. RESTRICTIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sure that while you have allowed a little leeway to the Leader of the Opposition to express himself briefly by way of a question, you would stop me from answering as fully in my reply. May I say I am very glad that the Hon. Mr. Kierans has found an acceptable place to express his views. So far as I am concerned, I am very glad that he has. I think this has been a useful contribution to the discussions. I know that the hon. gentleman will not expect me to deal in detail with his question, which would require me to make a speech. May I just say that with many of the things Mr. Kierans has said we would all agree.

subtopic: SPEECH BY QUEBEC MINISTER RESPECTING U.S. RESTRICTIONS
speechtext:
Which one?
February 2, 1966

Inquiries of the Ministry

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SPEECH BY QUEBEC MINISTER RESPECTING U.S. RESTRICTIONS
speechtext: I can make my speech now if you will give me the time. I should like to say that there are some points on which I do disagree with Mr. Kierans. If there is an opportunity this afternoon, perhaps I might make a few very brief comments during the debate on the supply motion, not to give a reply to Mr. Kierans but to indicate some of the points I think ought to be kept in mind.

subtopic: SPEECH BY QUEBEC MINISTER RESPECTING U.S. RESTRICTIONS
speechtext:
May
I ask a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker? In view of the very serious implications for the Canadian economy which Mr. Kierans has pointed out in great detail, does the minister not agree it is time to make a serious protest in this regard to the United States Secretary of Commerce?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SPEECH BY QUEBEC MINISTER RESPECTING U.S. RESTRICTIONS
speechtext: In reply may I say two things. First of all, as I said in my speech the other day, we expressed ourselves very strongly to the United States. We have not accepted the guide lines in any agreement reached between Canada and the United States. We are quite free to take whatever action we like. On the other hand, we did not feel that it was appropriate for us to make any concessions to the United States in order to buy our exemption from these guide lines. We think they should not be applied to Canada and hope the United States will come to that view.

subtopic: SPEECH BY QUEBEC MINISTER RESPECTING U.S. RESTRICTIONS
speechtext: May I ask a further supplementary question. Would the minister be willing to table his reply to the United States government for the information of the house?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SPEECH BY QUEBEC MINISTER RESPECTING U.S. RESTRICTIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think all there is on the record is a press statement I issued in which I set out the agreement and the statements made by the various secretaries in the United States. Perhaps the hon. gentleman could clarify his question.

subtopic: SPEECH BY QUEBEC MINISTER RESPECTING U.S. RESTRICTIONS
speechtext: Since there was nothing of a positive nature in the minister's statement to the United States Secretary of Commerce, will he please advise the house by tabling his reply exactly what he did say, if he did say anything at all?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SPEECH BY QUEBEC MINISTER RESPECTING U.S. RESTRICTIONS
speechtext: I deny the implication in this question. If I may be permitted to speak for just a moment, we made very vigorous representations to the United States on this question, as vigorous as Mr. Kierans has made.

subtopic: SPEECH BY QUEBEC MINISTER RESPECTING U.S. RESTRICTIONS
speechtext: Then table them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SPEECH BY QUEBEC MINISTER RESPECTING U.S. RESTRICTIONS
speechtext: I made a speech in this house in which I set them forth. They were not in writing. Why would they be in writing? I attended meetings with the Secretary of Commerce, I attended meetings with the Secretary of the Treasury, as did my officials. I gave a factual and clear account which I suggest my hon. friend should read before he makes these loose statements in this house.

subtopic: SPEECH BY QUEBEC MINISTER RESPECTING U.S. RESTRICTIONS
speechtext: I have read them and there is still nothing there.

subtopic: SPEECH BY QUEBEC MINISTER RESPECTING U.S. RESTRICTIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a further supplementary question. The Minister of Finance has said that we are perfectly free to take whatever action we choose with respect to the guide lines which have been established by the government of the United States. May I ask the minister what action the government proposes to take in the light of these guide lines?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SPEECH BY QUEBEC MINISTER RESPECTING U.S. RESTRICTIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if the guide lines have adverse effects upon Canada, or I should say if the United States guide lines have an adverse effect on Canada, and there is no evidence yet that they have-

subtopic: SPEECH BY QUEBEC MINISTER RESPECTING U.S. RESTRICTIONS
speechtext: They will.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SPEECH BY QUEBEC MINISTER RESPECTING U.S. RESTRICTIONS
speechtext: -then the Canadian government is quite prepared to issue its own guide lines if necessary. Long before Mr. Kierans ever interjected himself into this situation the governor of the Bank of Canada called in the heads of the chartered banks and spoke to them about the possibility that by reason of the guide lines some Canadian companies subsidiary to American companies might be operating in Canada to the detriment of other Canadian customers. If necessary we will take other measures. I can assure the hon. member that we will take steps, just as strong as the United States is taking to protect the interests of citizens of that country in order to protect the interests of Canadian citizens.

subtopic: SPEECH BY QUEBEC MINISTER RESPECTING U.S. RESTRICTIONS
speechtext:
A further supplementary
question, Mr. Speaker. May I ask the minister if the disagreement which he expressed to the representative of the United States government arose out of his fear that these guide lines would have some adverse effect on Canada? May I ask the minister why it is necessary to wait until those adverse effects are apparent rather than acting now?
February 2, 1966	COMMONS

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SPEECH BY QUEBEC MINISTER RESPECTING U.S. RESTRICTIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the reason we made those representations, and the foundation of our relations with the United States, is that Canada is not contributing to the difficulties of the United States. Therefore we urged the government of the United States in its own interest as well as in ours not to apply these guide lines to Canada. This is the basis of it. However, I do not think there is any evidence yet that these will have an undesirable effect. Indeed, there are some aspects of them that might be in accordance with our own policy. However, if they do have an adverse effect I can assure the hon. member that we are not going to stand idly by.

Can the Minister of Finance tell us if, in his meetings with the governor of the Bank of Canada, anything was said about using new capital from the Bank of Canada to make up for the capital which is no longer available in the United States?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Acting Prime Minister. We have learned during recent days more particularly that India is experiencing the worst famine of the century. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question concerns the central government's relations with Quebec and the latter's attitude toward Ottawa and the other provinces.
The recent demise of the Fulton-Favreau formula to amend the constitution which was rejected solely by Quebec, emphasizes the political and constitutional tensions which are tearing the country. One of the main reasons for the rejection of the formula by the people of Quebec is the central government's refusal to grant special status to Quebec.
When the present Prime Minister gave his interpretation of the Fulton-Favreau formula in a press release dated November 3, 1964, he said on page 4, paragraph G:
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
There is absolutely nothing in the provisions which gives directly or indirectly, implicity or explicity. a special status to any one province within the Canadian federation. It is equally impossible to contend that the delegation clause was written with that intent, since such delegation must have the consent of the federal parliament and of at least four provinces.
Why, Mr. Speaker, are the political and constitutional agreements of 1867 and the reality of 1966 stubbornly not recognized?
The day that a Canadian leader who neither uses ill-assorted tactics which create confusion nor takes an attitude of autocratic arrogance which prevents dialogue forms a team by appealing to right-thinking people and proposes a fair and realistic solution to our conflicts, then, Canadians from coast to coast will stop distrusting each other and the country will be able to make giant strides in a spirit of agreement and open co-operation.
Supply

Mr. Allard
Does the province of Quebec enjoy a special status, beside the ordinary provincial status, like the other provinces? I say yes, Mr. Speaker, mainly for the following reasons: first, Quebec is a province different from the others. To say that Quebec is different from the other provinces is not a reference in particular, to geographical features, its economy and its administration, because all the Canadian provinces have their own characteristics. This means rather that Quebec considers itself as the stronghold of the French Canadian people and that its inhabitants are raised with a different mentality, culture, education and institutions.
That is why, when Ottawa tries continuously to set up, in all respects, uniform administrative standards for the whole country, although these standards may respond quite well to the English Canadian mentality, Ottawa comes up against the French Canadian group which requires special consideration from the educational, cultural, social, civilian and professional standpoints. Besides, a particular status is nothing new; it was recognized in the very text of our Canadian constitution. Just like in 1774 and in 1791, by the Quebec Act and the Constitutional Act, the B.N.A. Act of 1867 acknowledged special privileges and consideration for the province of Quebec, because it is the national home of French Canadians.
Twelve sections of the B.N.A. Act bear witness to it, namely, section 22 (2), section 23 (6), sections 51, 71, 73, 80, 92, subsections 13, 93, 94, 98, 129 and 133. These sections deal with more particularly, the special qualifications of the senators from Quebec, the composition of the Quebec Legislative assembly, the special qualifications of the members of the Quebec legislative council, the fixed number of federal members from Quebec, the exclusive provincial authority in matters of ownership and civil law, authority made exclusive because of the demands of Quebec, the exclusive provincial authority in education, again because of the different characteristics of French Canadians in this respect, and the impossibility for Ottawa to give Quebec the same law as the other provinces, the necessity of choosing as judges of the Quebec courts members of the Bar of that province, the sole authority of the Quebec legislature to amend acts in force since 1774 and, finally, compulsory bilingualism in Quebec and Ottawa.

February 2, 1966
Supply-Mr. Allard
Even if section 133 of the constitution on bilingualism is mostly a guarantee for the English minority in Quebec, this section is no less a distinctive feature of our province.
Nowadays, we often see Ottawa passing bills suited to the way of life of English Canadians, while Quebec reacts differently because of its different mentality. Let us mention grants to universities, federal loans to students, school allowances, the pension plan, the opting out from joint programs; if my memory serves me well, the Quebec provincial government has withdrawn from 29 joint programs over the past few years. It always seems to be the only provincial government to do so. Then you have this special attitude, this constant, uniform and unilateral reaction of Quebec to the Fulton-Favreau formula and to the provinces' jurisdiction in international affairs.
This special status which is explicitly recognized in the British North America Act-that is in the constitution of our country-has taken larger proportions and has been more evident these past few years in the fields I have just mentioned and particularly so in regard to the following matters:
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
It can be said that this particular status, asked for by Quebec, deals with education, culture, social security, economic planning, taxation, authority in international matters, development of natural resources, repatriation of all Quebec subjects, including the Eskimos, and the fair delimitation of its territory, as well as the problems of the Que-bec-Labrador border.
This particular status keeps on expanding. We find it every week, often in the attitudes and the stands taken by the Premier of Quebec and his colleagues of the provincial cabinet.
They are trying to extend this particular status into the field of family allowances and social security pensions.
Hon. Rene Levesque, Minister for Family and Welfare, made the point clear. He said during his last visit here in Ottawa, while attending a federal-provincial conference, that it was Quebec's intention, especially as far as family allowances and old age pensions are concerned, to take over completely in the social field, in order to satisfy Quebec's aspirations and characteristics according to co-ordinated and efficient social tenets.

As explained by another Quebec minister, Hon. Pierre Laporte, this special status requires control over everything related to Quebec families and, indirectly, over mortgage loans and housing.
When we hear various Quebeckers and other public men in Quebec indicate the extent of this special status, they take position on the monetary policy, the indirect taxes, while insisting on a greater share of direct taxes, Quebec participation in federal organizations, such as the Bank of Canada, the Senate, a constitutional court, as well as a cultural medium through a Quebec radio and TV network.
Special status for Quebec, Mr. Speaker, takes the form of an unconditional fiscal equivalent. In many areas I have mentioned, other provinces than Quebec could choose such an equivalent, but because of their mentality, the majority of English speaking Canadians readily accept that Ottawa interfere in everything to influence the economy and the tax structure and to provide equal opportunities to rich and poor areas alike.
I feel that the present tax option is still a temporary device; it is too vague and too uncertain and it leads to an administrative mess.
I understand that, until now, that option has enabled Quebec to achieve special status by gradual occupancy. But the time has come for men of good faith and for courageous and responsible legislators to recognize and define the particular status of Quebec in a framework of dynamic Canadian federalism respectful of the pluralistic character of society.
In order to eliminate constant and divergent pressures, in order to lessen conflicts and misunderstanding, it is now desirable to set about writing a new constitution, which will give the country a positive and bicultural federalism and recognize for Quebec a particular status in some well-defined fields.
The proclamation of a particular status for Quebec cannot confine Quebeckers to a minority role, as was stated by the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Trudeau).
On the contrary-

The hon. member will notice that I have not yet resumed my seat, Mr. Speaker. According to the rules, he cannot make lengthy interjections. However, I urge him, after my brief remarks, to take the floor and to speak clearly and intelligibly for a change, as he claims that we have not correctly interpreted his attitude on the matter of a special status for the province of Quebec.
The premier of Quebec maintains, to the contrary, that a special status for Quebec would be a condition for Canada's survival, because the province of Quebec would then acquire a feeling of equality it does not have at this time, and things being straightened out, the two ethnic groups could operate a rapprochement that would humiliate nobody.
I hope that this statement of the premier of Quebec agrees with the feelings of the hon. member for Mount Royal, because personally, I must say that, according to the comments received by all the newspapers in and outside Quebec concerning this statement may by the premier in the Chamber of Commerce of Ste. Foy, he expressed very well the feelings of Quebeckers and French Canadians who wish to obtain a special status in a revised constitution adapted to the problems of 1966.
Mr. Speaker, I also wish to draw the attention of hon. members to the editorials in the newspaper Le Devoir for December 13, 1965, signed by a well known journalist, Mr. Claude Ryan, and in the Globe and Mail of December 11, 1965.
This is what the Toronto paper says about the special status of Quebec-if the hon. member for Mount Royal takes the floor later on, I would like him to tell us his reactions and comments concerning the opinion of English Canadians who already show a rather progressive attitude toward a Quebec reality within a new federation. I quote an extract of this article of the Globe and Mail dated December 11, 1965:

That this special status exists is now accepted by most informed Canadians, however grudgingly. Most also accept the necessity for a rewriting of the constitution, although what form this will take is still a matter for full debate... A redrawing of the Canadian constitution being inevitable,
Supply-Mr. Allard
however, what matters is how the task is approached. On the one side must be Quebecers with the positive attitude of Mr. Ryan, ready to discuss fairly without using the blackmail threat of separation. The others at the table must have left behind laments for the One Canada that might have been and must act realistically to meet the demands of the new Canadian federalism.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)

We must then, Mr. Speaker, define as soon as possible the special status of the province of Quebec so as to create more coherence and more serenity in Canada.
We are not short of suggestions since, on January 19,	1966, some hon. members
proposed in this house the setting up of a parliamentary committee or the calling of a constitutional conference. What has been the government's reaction until now? It has given no efficient answer to this urgent and basic problem concerning constitutional and political reactions. I hope it will not wait longer so that contempt and turpitude will not replace a true and definite rapprochement between the two great founding nations of our country. Mr. Speaker, it is not very pleasant to hear other members talking among themselves, when they could take the trouble to listen to what we have to say about the aspirations of the people of Quebec, who expect so much from legislators on this matter. When a member has taken the trouble to study the matter and is acting as the spokesman of his constituents, I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that members should listen and then take part in the debate.
This is a matter of vital importance. Too many Canadians from coast to coast are still asking: "What's going on in Quebec" and "What do they want".
Well, if you are interested to know why Quebeckers and French Canadians are dissatisfied, you should first listen and keep silent, consider the matter and have an exchange of views. This is an important problem. I see the member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette) who in this house and elsewhere has taken an attitude which often expresses the aspirations of his constituents and I congratulate him on it. I hope that he will listen to my speech instead of trying to interrupt me.

speechtext:
I know that the member for Mount Royal is eager to speak and we are

February 2, 1966
Supply-Mr. Allard,
eager to hear him, because his statement at the beginning of 1966, reported in several newspapers, has really spread consternation, not so much among his constituents of Mount Royal, who cannot represent a large part of French Canadians, but among the people of the province of Quebec and in the heart and mind of French Canadians.
The spontaneous outcry from the newspapers and the people interested in these matters was that the hon. member for Mount Royal-I hope he will appreciate this in a few moments, if he has not already done so-made a statement which runs counter to the views, the opinions, the wishes or the aspirations of the Quebec people and of the French Canadian nation. I am glad to be able to tell him that today in this house. The time has come for him to take his responsibilities, to stand up this afternoon and to tell us what he thinks of Quebec, and to what lengths he is prepared to go to give Quebec, in a renovated confederation, the vitality and the powers that belong to that province so that it can thrive, having obtained a fair and equal treatment.
Such are, Mr. Speaker, the remarks I find myself forced to make during my speech. I believe that answer is appropriate. I think certain hon. members should rise and speak this afternoon on those important matters. Be assured that those problems will not be settled automatically.
In this field the most noteworthy opinion came not from a Canadian but from an American university professor who, hardly one and a half years ago, came to Canada to witness at first hand that new and dynamic quality which is going to revitalize the province of Quebec, as well as to study Canadian political and constitutional problems. He spent three months of study and observation in Canada and in Quebec. I am referring to Professor Griffith, but I cannot remember the university to which he belongs. Here is the piece of advice which that foreigner, a realistic and practical man, not prejudiced against any school of thought, submitted at the close of his investigations: he tells English Canada to stop banking on the good old submissiveness of days gone by. Because there is less talk about separatism and less trouble, people think that the problems have been solved. It just is not true. I ask hon. members from other provinces to visit the riding of Sherbrooke, as well as the other ridings in Quebec, when the house is

not sitting or even during a week end. Whether they come from the Western provinces, the Maritimes or British Columbia, they are welcome to visit that beautiful riding which, like many others in the Eastern Townships, is an example of the true Canadi-anism which should actuate every Canadian.
As a matter of fact, the riding of Sherbrooke, located in the heart of the Eastern Townships, was dominated about a hundred years ago by the English element. Today, it is mostly French. But the two ethnic groups co-exist alongside many other ethnic groups which came to settle there. There is no problem, no conflict, no tension, no pressure. If Canada was like the riding of Sherbrooke, and other ridings in the Eastern Townships, you would not hear people say that the province of Quebec wants this or that or that Ottawa should do this and that.
From the day when it is no longer necessary to struggle in the midst of political and constitutional conflicts, Mr. Speaker, Canada will take gigantic steps toward understanding, fraternity and friendship.
The government and the members have to take their responsibilities and should not leave exclusively to royal commissions, working committees, newsmen and commentators the task of pondering on this question.
As legislators we have to consider the question. Now, during this session, and not in ten months but right now, the present government, which for three years showed goodwill toward these difficult problems, should establish a parliamentary committee, comprising members on both sides of the house, to study the research work undertaken by these commissions, and in so doing, promote a dialogue, in good faith, among legislators aware of their responsibilities.
If our only function here is to ratify statements made outside the house or prepared by various departmental officials, our role here is not justified and we might as well be replaced by robots. But we have not been elected for that purpose.
Nineteen hundred and sixty six will be a most important year; what with the Carter Commission's report and findings which experts are now examining, and the Quebec Belanger Commission's report which has just been referred to and which we have not read because it has not been distributed yet. This is apparently a voluminous and most interesting report.
There is a committee on the constitution in Quebec which has been operative for two
February 2, 1966

years. The Quebec government, seeing this problem cropping up, set up a committee on the Canadian constitution to define and detect the definite trend of Quebec's future within a Canadian confederation.

Here is a Quebec provincial government which, by the creation of a committee made up of government members and members of the opposition, discharges its responsibilities. Those legislators take up their responsibilities at the proper place, in the legislature and not in the halls and lobbies.
Well, Mr. Speaker, it is now our turn in Ottawa to act in the same way. A few days ago, at the time the Fulton-Favreau formula was buried, the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) indicated that the question, or this type of question, could well be referred to a parliamentary committee that would be created to study federal-provincial relations.
At last here is a statement that must be followed by positive action. By the end of this session in 10 or 12 months, or late in 1966, that is, after a hundred years of federative life, this question wil have to be settled.
We should not be too hard on the fathers of confederation. They attempted in good faith at a specific time to solve the problems of the day. They could not foresee everything on this Canadian soil. They could not foresee all kinds of inventions, the existence of oil and mining rights on the continental shelf, the advent of planes, radio and television. That is why a lot of things are not dealt with in the constitution of 1867, but are nevertheless in effect.
Well, it is for legislators of 1966 to think, to discuss, to dialogue, to define. We cannot continue in darkness. Even if you call that co-operative federalism, we just cannot limit ourselves to letting basic constitutional problems be solved by the fantasy of governments or politicians that succeed one another without any possibility of defining jurisdictions. That is what this country now lacks.
The federal government can be a strong and powerful central government. I suggest that it is important to define the measures which have been provided for by the 16 subjects- and probably others which have come up since then-contained in section 92 of the constitution.
Instead of the government saying simply that it wants to be a strong government, it should specify in what field it wants to be

strong in 1966. It can, now, be strong in new fields which the Fathers of Confederation could not foresee.
The province of Quebec and the other provinces want to become eventually strong and powerful. They want to flourish, not as mere offshoots, but as autonomous powers, ir the field of legislation and finance. It would also be useful to define the weaknesses of our national and provincial policy. First let us define our constitutional policy, so that politicians and federal and provincial legislators who want a bona fide understanding will be able to reach it.
We can travel from one end of the country to the other, to Vancouver, Halifax, Fredericton. Here we meet members from all parts of the country. We eat together, have a smoke or a chat together behind the curtains. So why not take advantage of this session to assume our responsibilities since we represent every part of the country?
Why not start, officially and not informally, by defining the orientation of our constitutional policy, in order to create a Canadian constitution and then establish the positive and cultural policy of which I indicated, on January 28, the ten main features, with a special status for Quebec.

Mr. Speaker, I intend to speak very briefly, as I said in reply to a question by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), to make a few points on the application and the implications of United States guidelines on direct investment in Canada. First of all, I should like to make it quite clear, as I think I did during the question period and as I did in a speech I gave earlier this session, that I am not defending the United States guidelines on direct investment. As Minister of Finance I advised the government of the United States that I thought they were unwise, both economically and politically, to apply these guidelines to Canada. Therefore in what I have to say I am maintaining the position that it would be in the interests of both Canada and the United States if Canada were exempt from these guidelines.
The first general point I should like to make is that in discussing the problem of the effect of these United States measures on Canada we must recognize that the United States has a balance of payments problem and that these guidelines, as well as other measures, are related to that problem alone. Now,

February 2, 1966
Supply-Mr. Sharp
some experts disagree as to the nature of the United States international financial problems. However, I believe we have to recognize that the United States must be the judge of its own responsibilities and its own position.
Undoubtedly the United States government is concerned about its balance of payments position. If it were not concerned, it would not be employing the extraordinary measures it is employing. This leads me to the second point and that is that one should not make the assumption that is sometimes made, I notice, that the United States government has embarked upon a new and permanent policy of guidelines on direct investment by international companies based in the United States. If that were so, if in fact we were convinced that the United States had embarked upon a new, permanent policy, there would be very serious cause for concern on the part of not only Canadians but the world at large.
For the time being at least I think one ought to give the benefit of the doubt to the United States government and accept the views expressed by members of that administration. If I may, I should like to quote the views expressed by Mr. Connor, Secretary of Commerce, on January 17 as reported in the New York Times of that day. He said that the voluntary balance of payments program should be ended by February of next year. The more important part of what he said is the following, as outlined in this article:
In discussing the ending of the nrogram a year from now. Mr. Connor said the government recognized that restraint on direct investment, in particular. was against the longer-run interest of the nation and of the balance of payments, because it would ultimately reduce both exports and income from investments.
On that point I think there is agreement between the government of the United States and the government of Canada, and even by Mr. Kierans, that these measures are not in the interests of the United States in the longer run. I think we must take it for granted that the United States has adopted these policies temporarily and that they are not part of a new orientation of United States thinking.
The third point, and one that I have emphasized before in this house but which I should like to emphasize again, is that it is in Canadian interests and in the interests of the western alliance that the United States should overcome its difficulties. Our attitude

as Canadians should be one of co-operation by all reasonable means. This does not mean we should be reluctant to express our views with frankness and vigour to the United States government, as we have done. I have no complaint at all about the fact that others in this country have been expressing very vigorous views about the application of these policies to Canada.
It does seem to me, however, that we should not go out of our way to increase the difficulties of the United States because we do want them to overcome their problems so that they can resume the policies they were following when there were no restraints on the movement of capital in or out of the United States.
Finally, I do wish to make it clear once again, as I did in answer to a question today, that the Canadian government did not accept the application of United States guidelines on direct investment to Canada. These guidelines on direct investment did not form any part of our understanding with the United States government. In December I announced the terms of the agreement with the United States government which related to access to the United States market for long term funds and freedom from the United States interest equalization tax, in return for which we agreed to try to achieve a target on our reserves. This was our agreement.
In so far as the guidelines are concerned, we are free to take whatever action seems to be appropriate to protect Canadian interests including, if necessary, as I suggested earlier today, guidelines of our own. For example, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters) at my suggestion is examining the effects of these guidelines upon the trade of Canada and will no doubt be talking to the heads of Canadian companies that might be affected by the guidelines applicable to their United States parents.
I intimated also in answer to a question today something about our attitude on the financial implications of these guidelines. I should like to amplify that. The United States balance of payments position is basically protected by the agreement on reserves. It would be most undesirable if the effect of the United States guidelines were to induce strong new pressures of a distorting sort on credit and capital markets in Canada. This would be harmful to Canada and in view of the over-all character of our arrangement
February 2, 1966

with the United States it would be of no benefit to that country since it would merely push Canadian borrowers into the new issue market in the United States.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
The Governor of the Bank of Canada on December 10, immediately after the publication of the American guidelines, informed the chief executive officers of the five largest Canadian banks that it was his hope and expectation that if the banks found themselves confronted with new applications for credit resulting from the American guidelines at a time when they were unable to meet in full the normal demands for business loans for credit-worthy customers, they would continue to look after customers who had relied on them in the past to meet their financial needs. The chief executive officers indicated that they agreed this was the proper course for them to follow. The governor's views were reiterated at a meeting with the chief executive officers of all the banks held on January 5.
So far as long term issues of American subsidiaries are concerned, I would hope and expect that there will be no abnormal recourse to the Canadian capital market, but if there were the government would have to decide what action to take. As I mentioned in my speech last Thursday, the United States new issue market is open to American subsidiaries as well as to other Canadian companies. If abnormal borrowing in our capital market developed, this would merely push other Canadian borrowers into the new issue market in the United States and so provide no benefit whatever to the United States balance of payments.
These are the general comments I wanted to make, Mr. Speaker, supplementary to the questions that I answered today. May I just say in conclusion that this is a time, as I said on an earlier occasion, for vigilance and watchfulness on the part of the Canadian government and indeed on the part of Canadians. May I suggest, in the interests of Canada and in the interests of helping the United States overcome its problems, which have repercussions upon us in Canada, that it is also a time for restraint, for forbearance and for understanding.

It would be interesting to have the minister explain what portion of Mr. Kierans' speech he does agree with, for the essence of
February 2, 1966

Mr. Kierans' speech was that this government has failed to protect the interests of Canadians. Let that be perfectly clear. I am not going to go into the question of loss of contracts by Canadian stamping companies because we brought that question up the other day. All along the line this government, in its desire to establish for itself the reputation of being filled with the milk of diplomacy, will accept anything, will stand for anything, and will go no further than to say in effect: "Now, if you don't watch out we have the right to act and we will act".

I now want to say a word regarding estimates generally and the responsibility of this House of Commons to look carefully into expenditures. The government takes the attitude that the major purpose of parliament is the passing of legislation even though every principle of political science and practical parliamentary government asserts that the major responsibility is the examination of supply. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) dealt with this matter yesterday.
Across this nation the Liberal party is spreading the propaganda that it is a questionable attitude by the opposition to move votes of non-confldence. They are assisted in this by some pundits close to the throne, who suggest that this is something abnormal, that what the opposition is doing in moving amendments is holding up parliament and preventing the government, which has no plan anyhow, from bringing in that which they have not got. The very paucity of their program is apparent from an examination of the Speech from the Throne. They are leaving the impression that here is a government
Supply-Mr. Diefenbaker which is trying to do something that the opposition is preventing it from doing because the opposition moves votes of nonconfidence.
If hon. gentlemen opposite would speak honestly, they would admit there is no way for an opposition to secure the opinion of parliament on matters which it believes it is necessary to raise in the interests of the country than to move a vote of non-confidence. There is no other medium. Do you hear Prime Minister Wilson of the United Kingdom complaining because regularly there are votes of non-confidence? Nothing of the kind. They are essential to government.
It was embarrassing to the government to have to vote on the question of old age pensions. It exacerbated their finer sensibilities. I realize how badly they feel, after the event, about their vote on the removal of the 11 per cent sales tax. These things embarrass. Because they embarrass them, Mr. Speaker, they engage in propaganda to the effect that there ought not to be votes of non-confidence.
I like to look at the record, Mr. Speaker. I know there are members who have just been elected to the House of Commons who have not read the record. They have lived the mythology of Liberalism. The record is clear. When we were a minority government in 1957-58, did the principle that votes of nonconfidence were improper apply? Did we ever raise objection when we were on a razor's edge? Not at all. As far as the Liberal party at that time was concerned, they did not move immediate votes of non-confidence but whenever votes were moved by another party the Liberal party found it necessary to vote against the government.
The government complains about the number of votes of non-confidence. Between October, 1957, and January, 1958, there were nine amendments and subamendments moved. Has parliament changed? Has this principle which has been accepted through the years suddenly been found to be such that it is necessary to cast it into the discard because it is embarrassing to a government? When did this reformation in their thinking take place?
In 1962-63 we were again in a minority position following the election in June. Did they have the same views then? During that period of time, Mr. Speaker, eight amendments and subamendments were moved in the house. When we had a very large majority in the House of Commons the Liberals

We agreed to dispense with four of them. There has been no examination of the $7 billion of expenditures in the last fiscal year except for a few hours spent on external affairs. Why? Because of the precipitous haste with which the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) rushed to the country on the basis of advice from pundits imported from abroad, from columnists and from Gallup pollsters. The government says: Do not have supply motions, they embarrass us, they hold up parliament, they interfere with a government full of vim and vigour. But no vitality. This is the kind of fiction they are indulging in. We have said we want to examine the accounts. We want to find out whether the money of the Canadian people is being wasted. Before starting the operation of a blueberry patch, a group of experts, including forestry engineers and agrologists, survey the lands where blueberries can be grown. They determine the condition of the forest, as well as the farming possibilities, and they provide an estimate of the cost for clearing and burning. This preliminary work is made at the request of regional unions of blueberry producers. As for the planning, it is done by members of the union, under the supervision of the staff of the district office, Colonization Branch, Department of Agriculture and Colonization.

They should pull out all stops, make the breathalizer test mandatory and increase the grant to the Canadian Highway Safety Council. A conference should also be called with provincial representatives, automobile manufacturer representatives and, in fact, representatives from all organizations willing to get together in a drive to bring about improvement in the situation.
Responsibility in highway safety has been ignored too long by all governments. Our laws and regulations have not kept pace with the times. Uniformity of laws and regulations, as well as of penalties, should apply to all provinces. Traffic signs and driver testing or any other feature having to do with our highways or driving on them should be the same.
Periodical vehicle inspection should be compulsory. Signboards, radio and television should be in constant use in an effort to keep all our people alert and aware of the need for extreme caution on our streets and highways. No doubt if the people I have suggested were brought together to set up a framework or a pattern for greater highway safety, many worthwhile ideas would be brought to light.
Automobile manufacturers have shown favourable response to highway safety through their willingness to supply cars for student training and supply them in abundance. Their designers are constantly investigating safety features and quite a number have been included in car equipment with satisfactory results. Perhaps the automobile people could be persuaded to go quite a lot further by way of extensive research on some of the recently suggested safety devices.
I suggest that in the not too distant future legislation will necessarily be passed to make anti-smog equipment a requirement. There is no way of assessing the injury being inflicted on us by carbon monoxide. However, we do know that any element that causes irritation in the lungs is a potential contributor to lung cancer. We know too that carbon monoxide is deadly when confined and may even be the cause of some highway accidents.
I take this opportunity to compliment the Canadian Highway Safety Council for their excellent effort over the years which has not been in vain but has been terribly handicapped by the lack of funds. The people who have kept the Highway Safety Council alive and active are all voluntary workers. Most of these people hold other quite responsible
Supply-Mr. Noble
positions in the business world so that work on the council is extra responsibility. Moral and financial support should be spontaneous and adequate. Instead, we find the council has run into frustrations in fund raising. Take this government, for example. The council has been unable to promote an increase of its grant from $25,000 per year for all types of safety, a problem that involved the death of
5.000	Canadians last year on highways alone.
By comparison, lung cancer killed less than
3.000	Canadians in 1964; yet this government spent almost $250,000 on an anti-smoking campaign. The council receives three times more support from industry than from the government. The casualty insurance industry, through the All Canada Insurance Federation, in support of one project alone, driver education, provides more funds than does the government of this nation. Another department of this government spent almost $100,000 for the production of a film on ballet dancing. There is no suggestion that these things are not worth while but it is abundantly clear, Mr. Speaker, that the grant to the Highway Safety Council is far out of perspective in comparison.
I mentioned before that 5,000 people were killed last year on the highways, and in addition 160,000 people were injured, many permanently. The net economic traffic accident loss to Canadians last year was approximately $4 billion.
I am most anxious, Mr. Speaker, to see the government give every aspect of this problem their very serious consideration. I feel they are duty bound to take immediate action. The people of this country are anxiously waiting an aggressive move and it must come from the top. As an illustration may I relate an experience I had last session. I asked two questions on motor vehicle safety. One was put on the order paper and the other on orders of the day. It so happened both were answered in Hansard on June 16. The one put on the order paper was as follows:
Has the government given consideration to introducing legislation making it compulsory to equip automobiles being sold in Canada with all safety devices currently proven practical and efficient?
The answer was given by the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury), who said:
It should be emphasized that the provincial governments have the responsibility of drafting and enforcing regulations pertaining to the operational standards of motor vehicles. A great deal of work has already been undertaken by various groups to determine the areas where improvement in design or vehicle construction could lead to

February 2, 1966
Supply-Mr. Noble
greater safety which would be useful In the preparation of a safety code. It would, of course, be necessary to obtain the agreement of the provinces before a uniform safety code could be established for motor vehicles. The Department of Industry would be happy to co-operate with the provinces in the preparation of such a code.
Now, Mr. Speaker, owing to the tact that the provinces were so prominently mentioned in this answer, I took the liberty of writing each provincial minister having jurisdiction over highway responsibilities in his respective province and asked for his deliberations on the matter in respect of my questions. Of course, I enclosed a copy of Hansard for June 16. Before parliament prorogued I had replies from six provinces indicating their willingness to proceed along any progressive line for more safety on our highways. These replies left no doubt in my mind as to the response that would be forthcoming if the senior government would show the way. In fact, several provinces in recent Throne Speeches have indicated they would make traffic law improvements. The following are excerpts from newspaper reports relating to Throne Speeches. First, from Ontario:
Ontario will almost triple the number of compulsory highway spot checks this year in an effort to reduce the traffic death toll, it was indicated Tuesday in the Throne Speech.
The government promised to operate compulsory motor vehicle inspection at 80 "floating" locations, an increase of 48 from 1965.
Instead of using fixed locations that motorists can easily avoid, mobile lanes for safety checks will be carried in trucks, and the locations changed regularly.
Deputy Transport Minister A. G. MacNab said the accelerated program will provide wide coverage of the province.
"With the motorist not knowing when and where he'll be checked, our hope is that all motorists will keep their cars in better shape," he said.
Then, from British Columbia:
The British Columbia government plans legislation for compulsory testing of motor vehicles and the ruling of impaired drivers off the road.
It also plans a royal commission into automobile insurance.
The speech gave no indication as to how impaired drivers would be dealt with. But it was learned authoritatively that a maximum level of alcohol in the blood would be set by law beyond which a driver would not be permitted to drive and it would be up to the driver to prove his non-intoxication by some sort of test. The type of test was not disclosed.
In May of this year the annual conference of the Canadian Highway Safety Council will be held in Calgary. This would be the logical time for the federal and provincial governments to launch a highway safety crusade which would embrace all interested people

and organizations with a view to making some realistic progress towards greater highway safety. However, it does seem to me that this government must take one major step previous to this meeting. I refer to clearing the deck on the alcoholic problem by an amendment to the Criminal Code making breathalizer tests mandatory.
Statistics bear out the fact that at least 50 per cent of all traffic accidents are caused directly by someone under the influence of alcohol. Many prominent people feel very strongly about this problem and here are some of the thoughts they have expressed as a result of their deliberations. These are the views of Mr. George B. McClellan, Commissioner of the R.C.M.P.:
Where are the civil rights of the family whose breadwinner has been cut down by some drunken sot in a high-powered car? What system exists to provide free legal advice to the widow who may have a legitimate civil claim for damages? Who moves in to rehabilitate her children, find them jobs, give them career guidance, feed them and clothe them? Who, indeed, but cold charity, and local welfare organizations?
But the drunk who drove the car, if convicted, is entitled to all these things when he becomes a ward of the state-
What about the right to insist that driving on our highways should be a reasonably safe pastime and not a competition to stay alive? It should not be necessary to spend every minute you are driving an automobile in endeavouring to outwit the nuts, the fireballs and the drunks who drive on every highway today without the slightest regard to life, regulation, safety or their fellow men.
This is what the Hon. Gordon Taylor has to say. He is the Highways Minister for Alberta, one of the ministers from whom I received a letter.
One drink before driving may soon be against the law, predicts Hon. Gordon Taylor, Alberta highways minister. The problem of drinking drivers is getting so bad it might get to the point where it will become an offence to drink at all and drive.
Under present legislation a drinking driver cannot be convicted unless police can establish impairment. Anti-drink-and-drive legislation will have to get stronger. At a conservative estimate, at least 50 per cent of today's highway accidents are caused because at least one person involved took a drink.
The minister said penalties against impaired drivers in Alberta are now among the highest in Canada.
Here is an opinion from Dr. Morton Shulman, Chief Coroner of Metropolitan Toronto.
More than half the drivers killed in Ontario car accidents between last November and this June had enough alcohol in their blood to be legally impaired, Metro Chief Coroner, Dr. Morton Shulman, said yesterday.
February 2, 196G

Urging that all drivers involved in accidents be given breath tests and that spot checks with breath testing machines be made. Dr. Shulman said only these steps would stop the slaughter on our highways.
Because forcing an individual to take the test might be objectionable to many, he recommended that applicants for a driver's license be required to sign a waiver allowing for tests. Such a system worked successfully in New York and other states, he said. If such a driver subsequently refused to allow a breath test, his license was cancelled.
The need was urgent, he said, because the people being killed were those in the prime of life. Quoting figures to emphasize the problem, Dr. Shulman said alcohol was involved in 50 per cent of all accidents producing fatalities. When one eliminates child pedestrian deaths, the alcohol factor may be as high as 80 per cent.
Dr. Shulman said he was suggesting the liberal use of breath tests in the hope that they would deter drivers from taking to the road after drinking, rather than in the hope more would be caught after doing so.
Chief Justice McRuer expressed himself as follows:
By logic these drinking drivers should not be judged by the results of their condition, but by the condition itself.
And that puts it on the basis that those who are impaired should all be treated severely. If we applied common sense in our society, that's precisely what would be done.
Anyone who drives on the highway in an impaired condition is a great menace to human life.
We wouldn't tolerate a man operating a crane on a construction job while his ability is impaired. He'd be dismissed at once. So would the impaired locomotive engineer on the railroad.
But in the public mind, impaired driving on the highway is a matter to be treated lightly. So that shows how illogical the public mind can be sometimes.
There's too light a value being placed on human life. All the focus in criminal auto accident cases before the courts is on the accused. The person whose life is destroyed is viewed very much as a mere statistic.
All of us are apt to have momentary lapses, to be thoughtless at times, to have our attention distracted. But that's quite different from undertaking to drive a dangerous thing like an automobile while under the influence of liquor, drugs or anything like that.
It is being accepted as a way of life, but I do not think it should be. I can't write the prescription to cure it, but if all segments of the public stirred themselves I think something could be done. The highway toll is not something we have to put up
Supply-Mr. Noble
with. If people obeyed the law accidents would be cut in half because most are due to people disobeying the rules of the road.
The alcohol problem was brought home to me forcibly a little over two weeks ago when within a few miles of my home a family of five people on their way home from church were all killed by a driver who had been drinking. This man received only minor injuries.
It is my hope that the government will not delay in introducing the necessary amendments to the Criminal Code respecting drunk driving. At this time I also bring to the attention of the house the lack of courtesy and indifference displayed by car drivers at the gates of this very building. I refer to the traffic coming off Metcalfe street on to Wellington. When the green light comes on many drivers do not wait for the pedestrians to cross but drive out and dodge through the people crossing the street. A start could be made at our very doors.
